Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Iraq's government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit to Washington amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, an Iraqi government spokesman said Tuesday. Students protest the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. Ali al-Dabbagh said the Iraqi government approved several amendments that were "necessary, essential and appropriate" to the draft status-of-forces agreement, which would set the terms for U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate on their presence expires at the end of this year. "The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests," al-Dabbagh said. It is unclear when al-Maliki will submit the changes to the draft document. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said that there was "great reluctance" to make any more changes to the agreement. However, senior U.S. officials -- speaking under the condition of anonymity -- are not ruling out possibly renegotiating parts of the deal with Iraq if the country's parliament does not approve it. The most vocal opponent of the draft security deal in Iraq has been the political party of radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which opposes any U.S. military presence in Iraq. U.S. military helicopters Tuesday flew over Baghdad's Mustansiriya University, where hundreds of students took part in a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement against the status-of-forces deal. "We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty," said law student Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, one of the demonstrators. Fellow demonstrator and law student Hisham Mohammed said the students plan to organize a sit-in and a strike across universities in Iraq to protest the agreement. The draft status-of-forces agreement, according to a copy obtained by CNN, calls for U.S. combat troops to be out of Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and out of the country entirely by December 31, 2011. The agreement allows for an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces' stay in Iraq, by agreement of both parties. It also allows the Iraqi government to ask "the United States government to leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces." Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces in Iraq has been a sticking point in the negotiation, with the U.S. side preferring that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. Baghdad had sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit major crimes in the course of their duties. Under the draft agreement, U.S. forces or contractors who commit "major and premeditated murders" while off duty and outside U.S. facilities would fall under Iraqi jurisdiction, according to the copy obtained by CNN. All other crimes -- and murders committed inside U.S. facilities or by on-duty forces -- would fall under American jurisdiction, the agreement says.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Iraq's government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit amendments to Washington regarding a draft security agreement with the United States, an Iraqi government spokesman announced Tuesday.

Students protested the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. "The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to present these amendments to the American side in order to reach a draft agreement that preserves the fundamental principles and sovereignty of Iraq, along with its paramount interests," al-Dabbagh stated.

The timeline for al-Maliki's submission of these changes remains uncertain. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently indicated "great reluctance" toward making further modifications to the agreement. Nevertheless, senior U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, have not ruled out the possibility of renegotiating portions of the deal should Iraq's parliament fail to ratify it.

The most vocal opposition to the draft security agreement within Iraq has come from the political faction aligned with radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which rejects any continued U.S. military presence in the country. On Tuesday, U.S. military helicopters flew over Baghdad's Mustansiriya University, where hundreds of students gathered for a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement in protest of the agreement.

"We oppose this agreement between the Iraqi government and the American government because it violates Iraqi sovereignty," said Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, a law student among the demonstrators. Fellow protester and law student Hisham Mohammed indicated that students intend to organize sit-ins and strikes across Iraqi universities in continued protest of the agreement.

According to a copy obtained by CNN, the draft status-of-forces agreement stipulates that U.S. combat troops withdraw from Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and depart the country entirely by December 31, 2011. The agreement permits either an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces' presence, contingent upon mutual consent between both parties. It further allows the Iraqi government to request that "the United States government leave certain forces for training and support purposes for the Iraqi forces."

Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces stationed in Iraq has emerged as a critical point of contention throughout the negotiations, with American representatives advocating that their troops and contractors retain immunity from Iraqi law. For its part, Baghdad has sought authority to arrest and prosecute Americans accused of crimes unrelated to official military operations, as well as jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit serious offenses in the course of their duties.

Under the terms of the draft agreement, U.S. forces or contractors who commit "major and premeditated murders" while off duty and outside American facilities would fall under Iraqi jurisdiction, according to the copy obtained by CNN. All other offenses—along with murders committed within U.S. facilities or by personnel on active duty—would remain under American jurisdiction, per the agreement's terms.

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** — According to a spokesman for the Iraqi government, officials have given Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki the green light to present Washington with revisions to a proposed security pact between the two nations, it was announced Tuesday.

Students gathered Tuesday at Mustansiriya University in Baghdad to voice their opposition to the status-of-forces agreement. Spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh explained that the cabinet had signed off on a set of changes deemed "necessary, essential and appropriate" for the draft pact, which outlines how American troops would operate in Iraq once the U.N. mandate authorizing their presence lapses at year's end.

"The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests," al-Dabbagh stated. No timeline has been given for when al-Maliki intends to present these revisions to American counterparts.

Robert Gates, the U.S. Secretary of Defense, recently indicated there was strong hesitancy about introducing further modifications to the agreement. That said, unnamed senior American officials have left open the possibility of reworking certain provisions should Iraq's legislature fail to ratify the pact as it stands.

Among Iraqi factions, the fiercest resistance to the security arrangement has come from followers of firebrand Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose political movement rejects any continued American military footprint in the country.

Overhead, U.S. military helicopters circled above Mustansiriya University on Tuesday as several hundred students—mobilized by the Sadrist movement—staged a protest against the proposed deal. "We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty," declared Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, a law student participating in the rally. Another protester, law student Hisham Mohammed, indicated that students were planning coordinated strikes and sit-ins at universities nationwide to oppose the pact.

A copy of the draft agreement reviewed by CNN specifies that American combat forces must withdraw from Iraqi urban centers and towns by July 30, 2009, with a complete pullout from the country required by the end of 2011. The document does leave room for adjustment—either an accelerated departure or a prolonged stay—contingent on mutual consent between the two governments. It further stipulates that Iraqi authorities may formally request that Washington keep certain units in place to provide training and support to Iraqi security forces.

One of the thorniest issues throughout negotiations has centered on legal authority over American personnel stationed in Iraq. U.S. negotiators have pushed to keep their troops and contractors shielded from prosecution under Iraqi law, whereas Baghdad has pressed for the right to detain and prosecute Americans implicated in crimes unrelated to sanctioned military duties, as well as authority over service members and contractors who commit serious offenses while carrying out their assignments.

Per the document obtained by CNN, the compromise reached would place American forces or contractors under Iraqi legal jurisdiction specifically in cases of "major and premeditated murders" committed while off-duty and away from U.S. installations. Any other offenses—along with killings that occur on American bases or are committed by personnel actively on duty—would remain subject to U.S. legal authority.

# Iraq Seeks Amendments to U.S. Security Agreement Amid Domestic Pressure

Iraq's government has taken a significant step in the ongoing negotiations over the future of American military presence in the country, formally authorizing Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit a series of amendments to the draft security agreement with the United States. This decision reflects the government's efforts to address concerns regarding the terms governing U.S. troop presence within Iraqi territory.

Officials characterized these proposed amendments as "necessary, essential and appropriate," emphasizing that such changes are critical to safeguarding Iraq's sovereignty and upholding the country's fundamental national principles as negotiators work toward finalizing the agreement. This language underscores the delicate balance Iraqi leadership must strike between maintaining a security partnership with Washington and asserting full control over domestic affairs.

The urgency behind these negotiations stems from a looming deadline: the United Nations mandate authorizing the presence of foreign troops in Iraq is set to expire at the end of the year. Without a new bilateral agreement in place, there would be no legal framework to govern the continued presence of U.S. forces, making the status-of-forces agreement a critical and time-sensitive matter for both governments.

On the American side, however, there appears to be limited appetite for further concessions. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has expressed reluctance to entertain additional changes to the draft agreement, signaling that Washington views the current terms as largely settled. Despite this official stance, anonymous senior U.S. officials have hinted that the door to renegotiation might not be entirely closed—suggesting that should Iraq's parliament ultimately reject the deal, the United States could be compelled to return to the negotiating table.

Meanwhile, domestic opposition to the agreement has begun to manifest in visible public demonstrations. Hundreds of students, mobilized by the Sadr movement, gathered to protest the deal at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. These demonstrators view the agreement as an infringement on Iraqi sovereignty, reflecting broader unease among segments of the population regarding continued foreign military presence. Organizers have signaled that this protest is only the beginning, with plans already in motion for additional sit-ins and strikes to be staged across university campuses throughout the country, suggesting that the political and social debate over the agreement is likely to intensify in the weeks ahead.

# Iraq's Cabinet Authorizes Amendments to US Security Pact Amid Growing Opposition

Iraq's government has granted Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki the authority to propose further amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, a document that would establish the legal framework governing the presence of American troops in Iraq once the current United Nations mandate expires at the end of the year. The move comes as the agreement faces mounting political resistance domestically, underscoring the delicate and contentious nature of negotiations over the future of the U.S. military presence in the country.

The draft agreement, which has already undergone several rounds of revision, has become a lightning rod for political opposition within Iraq. Chief among the critics is the movement led by influential Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose followers view the pact as a violation of Iraqi sovereignty and an extension of foreign occupation under a different legal guise. Sadr's political bloc has mobilized public opposition to the deal, and in a visible demonstration of this discontent, his supporters staged protests at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. The demonstrations reflect broader anxieties among segments of the Iraqi population who fear that the agreement could enshrine long-term American military influence in Iraq well beyond the formal end of the occupation.

Al-Maliki's government now finds itself navigating a difficult balancing act: securing an agreement that satisfies Washington's strategic and legal requirements for maintaining troop levels and operational latitude, while also addressing the concerns of Iraqi lawmakers and factions who insist on stronger guarantees of sovereignty, clearer timelines for troop withdrawal, and greater Iraqi legal jurisdiction over American forces operating within the country's borders. The authorization to propose amendments suggests that the Iraqi government recognizes it may need to extract further concessions from Washington in order to secure the necessary parliamentary support for ratification.

On the American side, the response to potential changes has been mixed. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates signaled reluctance to reopen the agreement for substantial renegotiation, expressing concern that additional revisions could unravel the delicate compromises already reached after months of difficult talks. Gates's comments reflect a broader unease within the Pentagon and parts of the Bush administration about prolonging the negotiation process, particularly as the deadline tied to the expiration of the UN mandate draws closer.

However, this position was not universally shared across the administration. Unnamed senior U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, indicated a greater degree of flexibility, suggesting that Washington would be willing to consider further changes to the agreement if it became clear that the Iraqi parliament would otherwise reject it outright. This acknowledgment reveals a pragmatic recognition within U.S. policy circles that failing to secure parliamentary approval would leave the legal status of American troops in Iraq in serious jeopardy once the UN mandate lapses, potentially forcing an abrupt and legally ambiguous withdrawal or continuation of operations.

The tension between these two positions—Gates's caution against further amendments and other officials' willingness to entertain them—illustrates the precarious political standing of the security agreement on both sides of the negotiating table. For the United States, the stakes involve preserving operational flexibility for its military forces and safeguarding the strategic gains of the years-long engagement in Iraq. For Iraq, the negotiations have become a defining test of the country's ability to assert genuine sovereignty in shaping the terms of its relationship with a foreign military power that has occupied its territory for years.

Ultimately, the unfolding debate over the security agreement highlights how central the question of sovereignty has become in Iraqi politics as the country moves toward the next phase of its relationship with the United States. Whether the current draft, even with amendments, can secure the necessary support in Iraq's fractious parliament remains uncertain, but the intensity of the domestic opposition—exemplified by the demonstrations at Mustansiriya University—signals that any final agreement will need to more convincingly address Iraqi concerns about long-term foreign military presence if it is to achieve durable political legitimacy.

# Baghdad: A City Shaped by History and Resilience

Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, stands as one of the world's most historically significant cities. Founded in 762 AD along the banks of the Tigris River, it once served as the intellectual and cultural center of the Islamic Golden Age, home to the legendary House of Wisdom where scholars translated and expanded upon Greek, Persian, and Indian knowledge.

In recent decades, Baghdad has frequently appeared in international news coverage, with outlets like CNN reporting extensively on the city's transformation through periods of conflict, political change, and reconstruction. Since the 2003 invasion, Western media coverage has documented everything from the fall of Saddam Hussein's government to the challenges of establishing new governmental institutions, the rise and fall of extremist groups, and the ongoing efforts to rebuild infrastructure and civil society.

CNN's reporting from Baghdad has often provided viewers around the world with firsthand accounts of life in the city—capturing both moments of crisis and instances of everyday resilience among its residents. Correspondents stationed in Iraq have covered military operations, humanitarian concerns, and the perspectives of Iraqi citizens navigating profound changes to their communities.

Despite the challenges of past decades, Baghdad continues to hold deep cultural significance. Its historic sites, including ancient mosques, markets, and museums, reflect centuries of civilization. The city's residents have shown remarkable determination in rebuilding neighborhoods, restoring cultural institutions, and working toward greater stability.

Today, Baghdad represents both the complexities of Iraq's recent history and the enduring spirit of a population working to reclaim normalcy and prosperity. As international attention has shifted over the years, the city continues its ongoing story of recovery, blending ancient heritage with the realities of contemporary Middle Eastern geopolitics.

**Iraq's Cabinet Approves Amendments to U.S. Security Pact Amid Student Protests**

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Iraq's Cabinet approved a package of amendments Sunday to the proposed security agreement with the United States, a move officials hope will pave the way for approval by parliament, even as demonstrations against the pact continued to flare on university campuses across the capital.

The revised text of the agreement, which would govern the presence of U.S. troops in Iraq once the current United Nations mandate expires at the end of the year, was passed by the Council of Ministers after weeks of negotiations between Baghdad and Washington over language addressing Iraqi sovereignty concerns.

Government spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh said the amendments reflect "the will of Iraqis" and address key sticking points, including provisions on the jurisdiction over U.S. soldiers and contractors accused of crimes, the timeline for a full American withdrawal, and guarantees that U.S. forces would not use Iraqi soil to launch attacks on neighboring countries.

"This agreement, with the changes that have been made, protects Iraqi sovereignty while allowing for a responsible transition as our own security forces take on greater responsibility," al-Dabbagh told reporters following the Cabinet session.

The pact must still be ratified by Iraq's 275-member parliament, where it faces opposition from lawmakers loyal to radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, as well as some Sunni and secular blocs who argue the agreement does not go far enough in setting a firm withdrawal date or limiting American military authority.

**Students Take to the Streets**

Opposition to the agreement was also visible Sunday at Mustansiriya University in Baghdad, where hundreds of students gathered to protest the pact, chanting slogans against the continued U.S. military presence and burning symbolic effigies of American flags, according to witnesses.

Demonstrators carried banners reading "No to Occupation" and "Iraq Says No to the Agreement," with organizers saying the protest was intended to pressure lawmakers ahead of the parliamentary vote.

"We reject any agreement that allows foreign troops to remain on our soil," said one student protester, who declined to give his name for fear of reprisal. "This is not liberation. This is prolonged occupation dressed in new language."

University security and Iraqi police monitored the demonstration, which organizers said was largely peaceful, though tensions rose briefly when a smaller group of counter-demonstrators expressing support for the government's position clashed verbally with protesters.

Mustansiriya University, one of Iraq's largest and oldest public universities, has been a frequent site of political activism since the fall of Saddam Hussein's government in 2003, with students representing a broad cross-section of Iraq's sectarian and political landscape.

**A Divisive National Debate**

The security agreement has become one of the most contentious political issues in Iraq since the war began, exposing deep divisions over the country's relationship with Washington. Supporters argue the pact is necessary to maintain stability during the transition of security responsibilities to Iraqi forces, while critics see it as a codification of a long-term American military footprint in the country.

Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki's government has pushed for swift ratification, warning that failure to approve the agreement before the U.N. mandate expires December 31 could create a legal vacuum for the roughly 150,000 U.S. troops still stationed in Iraq.

Al-Maliki is expected to present the amended agreement to parliament this week, though it remains unclear whether he has secured enough votes for passage. Some analysts say a national referendum, as stipulated under a compromise reached with parliamentary blocs, may ultimately be required to grant the pact full legitimacy in the eyes of the Iraqi public.

The Bush administration, which negotiated the original terms of the agreement, has signaled openness to the amendments, with U.S. officials saying they remain "cautiously optimistic" the pact can be finalized before the end-of-year deadline.

As the political process continues in the Green Zone, the scenes at Mustansiriya University served as a reminder of the deep public skepticism that persists on Iraqi streets — a sentiment that lawmakers will have to reckon with regardless of how the parliamentary vote unfolds.

*CNN's Baghdad bureau contributed to this report.*

# Iraqi Government Approves Revised Security Pact With United States

**BAGHDAD** — Iraq's cabinet has approved a revised draft of the long-negotiated security agreement with the United States, clearing a major hurdle in efforts to establish a legal framework governing the presence of American forces in Iraq after the expiration of the current United Nations mandate.

## Key Provisions

According to officials familiar with the agreement, the revised text sets a firm timeline for the withdrawal of U.S. combat troops from Iraqi cities, towns, and villages by June 30, with a complete withdrawal of all American forces from the country by the end of 2011. Iraqi officials have emphasized that these dates represent a "timeline" rather than a conditions-based drawdown, addressing longstanding demands from Baghdad for a definitive end to the foreign military presence.

## Jurisdiction Remains Contentious

Among the most difficult issues addressed in the negotiations was the question of legal jurisdiction over U.S. military personnel and contractors operating in Iraq. The revised draft reportedly grants Iraq jurisdiction over American soldiers and contractors who commit "serious crimes" while off-duty and outside U.S. military bases. This represents a significant shift from earlier positions and reflects sustained pressure from Iraqi lawmakers and the public, many of whom have pushed for greater sovereignty over legal matters involving foreign forces on Iraqi soil.

U.S. officials have historically sought to protect American personnel from prosecution under the Iraqi legal system, citing concerns about due process and the reliability of Iraq's judicial institutions. The compromise reached in this draft suggests both sides made concessions to reach consensus.

## Path Forward

The agreement now moves to the Iraqi parliament, where it faces additional scrutiny from various political blocs, including followers of cleric Moqtada al-Sadr and other factions that have historically opposed any extended U.S. military presence. Approval by parliament is not guaranteed, and further amendments could still emerge during legislative debate.

The pact is intended to replace the current U.N. Security Council mandate authorizing the U.S. military presence, which is set to expire at the end of the year. Failure to reach an agreement before that deadline could create legal ambiguity regarding the status of American forces in Iraq.

## Reactions

Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government has portrayed the revised deal as a victory for Iraqi sovereignty, while U.S. officials have characterized it as a workable framework that maintains necessary protections for American forces while respecting Iraq's legal system.

Analysts note that the coming weeks will be critical, as parliamentary debate could either solidify the agreement or send negotiators back to the table ahead of the year-end deadline.

*This is a developing story.*

# Iraqi Lawmakers, Students Voice Opposition to U.S. Security Pact

**BAGHDAD** — Political factions across Iraq's fractured parliament expressed sharp divisions Thursday over a proposed security agreement with the United States, as several hundred university students staged a demonstration near Baghdad University demanding the deal be scrapped entirely.

The draft agreement, which would govern the legal status of American forces and set conditions for their eventual withdrawal, has become a lightning rod for nationalist and religious groups who argue it compromises Iraqi sovereignty.

Followers of Shiite cleric Moqtada al-Sadr have been among the most vocal critics, organizing protests in Baghdad and several southern provinces. Sadrist lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session this week, denouncing the pact as an "occupation agreement in disguise."

"This is not a partnership between equals," said one Sadrist bloc member who declined to be named ahead of further negotiations. "Any document that allows foreign troops to operate on Iraqi soil without full accountability to our courts is unacceptable."

Sunni and Kurdish blocs have offered more measured responses, with some lawmakers suggesting the agreement is necessary to maintain stability while Iraqi security forces continue to develop. Others have called for amendments strengthening Iraqi judicial oversight of U.S. military personnel and setting firmer withdrawal timelines.

At the student demonstration, organized loosely through word of mouth and mosque announcements, young Iraqis voiced frustration that extended beyond the technical details of the pact.

"We were born into war, and now they want to make it permanent with paperwork," said Ahmed Kamal, a 21-year-old engineering student, holding a hand-lettered sign. "Six years is enough. We want them gone, not given a new legal reason to stay."

Another student, Zainab al-Rubaie, studying law, said she worried the agreement would be finalized without adequate public debate.

"Nobody asked us," she said. "This affects our generation the most, and the negotiations are happening behind closed doors, between men who won't have to live with the consequences."

Not all demonstrators called for an immediate American withdrawal, however. Some expressed ambivalence, fearing a security vacuum if U.S. forces departed too quickly.

"I don't love that they're here," said Hussein Jabbar, a 23-year-old economics student. "But I remember what the city looked like in 2006. I am afraid of what happens if they leave with nothing in place."

The Iraqi government has said it hopes to finalize the agreement before a United Nations mandate authorizing the U.S. military presence expires at the end of the year, though officials have acknowledged that securing parliamentary approval remains uncertain given the depth of public and political opposition.

Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's office did not respond to requests for comment Thursday, though government spokesmen have previously said any final agreement would "protect Iraqi sovereignty and dignity" while ensuring continued security cooperation.

*— Staff correspondent, Baghdad*

# U.S.-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement: Jurisdiction Disputes and Withdrawal Timeline Shape Contentious Negotiations

The Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) negotiated between the United States and Iraq, which took effect January 1, 2009, set binding timelines for the withdrawal of American troops while establishing controversial provisions regarding legal jurisdiction over U.S. military personnel and contractors operating in Iraq.

## Withdrawal Deadlines

The agreement established concrete deadlines for American military withdrawal following years of ambiguity about U.S. troop presence in Iraq. Under the pact's terms, U.S. combat forces were required to withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns, and villages by June 30, 2009, with a complete withdrawal of all U.S. forces from Iraqi territory mandated by December 31, 2011.

Then-Defense Secretary Robert Gates was among the key administration officials who addressed the practical and political dimensions of the agreement's timeline. Gates emphasized that the withdrawal schedule was tied to conditions on the ground and Iraqi security force readiness, while also framing the deadlines as firm commitments reflecting Iraqi sovereignty. He noted that the timelines represented a negotiated compromise designed to give Iraqi leadership confidence that the American military presence was not open-ended, while preserving enough flexibility for U.S. commanders to manage the transition responsibly.

Gates and other Pentagon officials also addressed concerns from military commanders about the operational risks of a fixed timeline, stressing that the agreement included mechanisms for consultation between the two governments should conditions require adjustments.

## Legal Jurisdiction Disputes

Among the most contentious elements of the negotiations was the question of legal jurisdiction over U.S. troops and Defense Department contractors. Under the finalized agreement, Iraq secured the right to prosecute American service members in certain circumstances—a significant shift from earlier arrangements under the Coalition Provisional Authority, which had granted U.S. personnel broad immunity from Iraqi law.

The final text specified that Iraqi courts would have jurisdiction over U.S. forces and contractors for major, premeditated crimes committed while off-duty and off-base, a narrower scope than initial Iraqi demands for comprehensive legal authority over American personnel. U.S. negotiators worked to ensure that service members acting in their official duties remained under American military jurisdiction, a distinction that became a central sticking point throughout the talks.

Iraqi officials had pushed for broader jurisdictional authority as a matter of national sovereignty, while American negotiators sought to protect troops from what they characterized as an unpredictable Iraqi legal system. The compromise reached was viewed by many analysts as a notable concession by Washington, reflecting the shifting balance of leverage as Iraqi political leaders faced domestic pressure to demonstrate sovereignty over foreign forces operating in their country.

## Sadr Movement Opposition

The agreement faced vocal opposition from followers of Shiite cleric Moqtada al-Sadr, whose political bloc organized demonstrations against the pact both before and after its ratification by the Iraqi parliament. Sadrist lawmakers and supporters criticized the agreement as insufficient in curtailing American military authority and argued that it failed to guarantee a genuine and complete end to foreign occupation.

Protesters aligned with the Sadr movement took to the streets in Baghdad and other cities, including demonstrations in Sadr City, denouncing the deal as a continuation of U.S. dominance over Iraqi affairs. Sadrist parliamentarians voted against the agreement when it came before the Council of Representatives, arguing that the withdrawal deadlines lacked sufficient guarantees and that the jurisdictional carve-outs for U.S. forces represented an infringement on Iraqi sovereignty.

Despite the Sadrist opposition, the Iraqi parliament approved the agreement by a majority vote, with the government of then-Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki arguing that the pact represented the best available mechanism for asserting Iraqi authority while ensuring a responsible transition of security responsibilities from American to Iraqi forces.

## Broader Implications

The SOFA's provisions were widely viewed as a significant milestone in the transition of authority from American to Iraqi institutions after years of a large-scale U.S. military presence following the 2003 invasion. The jurisdictional compromises and firm withdrawal deadlines reflected both the political pressures facing the Iraqi government to demonstrate sovereignty and the Bush administration's desire, in its final months, to formalize a legal framework governing the American presence ahead of the transition to the incoming Obama administration.

The debate surrounding the agreement—particularly the jurisdictional questions and the reaction from Sadrist factions—underscored the deep divisions within Iraqi politics over the terms of the American military's continued presence and eventual departure from the country.
